item.title: [Real Estate 101 #14] Your Property Sends You Two Tax Bills — One Every Year, One Only Once
item.body:
> Owning real estate means paying tax while you hold it and tax when you sell it — and good management is largely the work of shrinking both without shrinking the asset.

## Today's Concept

Most people think of a property as a thing you buy. In practice it's a small business you run, and like any business it has an operating side and a tax side.

**The operating side: property management vs. asset management.**

*Property management* is the day-to-day: finding tenants, collecting rent, fixing the water heater at 11 p.m., handling turnovers, keeping the building code-compliant. In the U.S., a residential property manager typically charges **8–10% of collected rent**, often plus a leasing fee of half to one month's rent each time a unit turns over.

*Asset management* is the level above it: Should we hold or sell? Refinance? Spend $40,000 on a kitchen renovation to push rents, or spend nothing and harvest cash? Property management protects the income; asset management decides what the income is *for*.

Both are measured through one number: **Net Operating Income (NOI)**.

```
NOI = effective gross income − operating expenses
```

Operating expenses include property taxes, insurance, maintenance, management fees, and utilities you cover. They **exclude** your mortgage payment and depreciation. That's deliberate — NOI describes the property, not your financing.

**The tax side: two very different bills.**

**1) The annual bill — property tax (the "holding tax").** In the U.S. this is levied locally, not federally: by counties, cities, and school districts. The county assessor sets an *assessed value*, and a tax rate (often quoted in *mills* — dollars per $1,000 of value) is applied to it. Effective rates vary enormously — roughly 0.3% of market value in Hawaii to well over 2% in New Jersey and parts of Illinois and Texas. On the same $400,000 house, that's the difference between about $1,200 and $8,800 a year, every year, forever.

Two things worth knowing: most states offer a **homestead exemption** that reduces the taxable value of your primary residence, and every state has a formal **assessment appeal** process. Some states also cap how fast assessed value can rise — California's Proposition 13 limits the increase to 2% per year until the property sells, at which point it's reassessed at market value.

**2) The one-time bill — capital gains tax (the "transfer tax").** When you sell, you're taxed on the *gain*, not the sale price:

```
gain = amount realized (sale price − selling costs) − adjusted basis
adjusted basis = purchase price + capital improvements − depreciation taken
```

Hold longer than one year and the gain gets **long-term capital gains** rates (0%, 15%, or 20% federally, depending on income), plus a possible 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax at higher incomes, plus state tax. Sell within a year and it's taxed as ordinary income — a materially worse outcome.

**The wrinkle that surprises everyone: depreciation recapture.** While you own a rental, the IRS lets you deduct the *building* (never the land) over **27.5 years** for residential property or **39 years** for commercial — a paper expense that shelters real cash income. But at sale, the depreciation you took gets pulled back into the gain as *unrecaptured Section 1250 gain*, taxed at up to 25%. Depreciation is a deferral, not a gift. And here's the trap: the IRS computes recapture on depreciation "allowed or allowable" — you owe it whether or not you actually claimed the deduction.

Three legal off-ramps are worth knowing by name:

- **Section 121 exclusion** — sell your *primary residence* after living in it 2 of the last 5 years and exclude up to **$250,000** of gain (single) or **$500,000** (married filing jointly).
- **Section 1031 like-kind exchange** — on *investment* property, roll the proceeds into another investment property and defer the gain. Strict clock: identify replacement property within **45 days**, close within **180 days**, and a qualified intermediary must hold the money. Since 2018 this applies to real property only.
- **Step-up in basis at death** — heirs generally inherit at fair market value, which can erase decades of embedded gain.

## In Everyday Life

Say you buy a single-family rental in Columbus, Ohio for **$300,000**. The county allocates $60,000 to land and $240,000 to the building. You put $150,000 down and borrow $150,000 at 6.5%.

**Year one, the operating side:**

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Gross rent ($2,200 × 12) | $26,400 |
| Less vacancy (5%) | −$1,320 |
| **Effective gross income** | **$25,080** |
| Property tax | −$4,500 |
| Insurance | −$1,400 |
| Management (9%) | −$2,257 |
| Repairs & maintenance | −$2,000 |
| **NOI** | **$14,923** |

Your mortgage costs about $948/month, or $11,377/year. So your actual **cash flow is about $3,546**.

**Now the tax side of the same year:**

```
NOI                          $14,923
− mortgage interest          $ 9,700   (principal is not deductible)
− depreciation ($240k/27.5)  $ 8,727
= taxable rental income     −$ 3,504
```

You put roughly $3,500 of cash in your pocket and report a **$3,500 loss**. That gap is depreciation doing its job. (Whether you can *use* that loss is a separate question — rental losses are generally "passive," though there's a special allowance of up to $25,000 for active participants, which phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of modified AGI.)

One nice detail: property taxes on a *rental* are an ordinary business expense on Schedule E and are **not** subject to the SALT cap that limits state and local tax deductions on your personal return. The same dollar of property tax is treated very differently depending on whether you live in the house or rent it out.

**Ten years later, you sell for $400,000** with 6% selling costs:

```
Amount realized    $400,000 − $24,000 = $376,000
Depreciation taken $8,727 × 10        = $ 87,270
Adjusted basis     $300,000 − $87,270 = $212,730
Total gain                              $163,270
   of which $87,270 is recapture       (up to 25%)
   and      $76,000 is long-term gain  (0/15/20%)
```

Notice: the property appreciated $100,000, but your taxable gain is $163,270. The extra $63,000-odd is the bill for ten years of depreciation deductions coming due — which is precisely why 1031 exchanges exist.

## Three-Line Recap

1. Property management protects NOI day to day; asset management decides when to hold, improve, refinance, or sell.
2. Property tax is local, annual, and permanent — effective rates range from under 0.5% to over 2% of value, so the *location* of a purchase is also a tax decision.
3. Capital gains tax is computed on gain over adjusted basis, and depreciation lowers that basis — so the deduction you enjoy while holding is largely a deferral you settle at sale.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**1.** Which of the following is **excluded** from operating expenses when calculating NOI?
  a) Property taxes   b) Property management fees   c) Mortgage principal and interest   d) Landlord-paid insurance

**2.** True or False: Residential rental buildings are depreciated over 27.5 years, and the land is depreciated over the same period.

**3.** You bought a rental for $300,000, made $20,000 of capital improvements, and took $50,000 of depreciation. What is your adjusted basis?
  a) $230,000   b) $270,000   c) $300,000   d) $370,000

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **NOI (Net Operating Income)** — Effective gross income minus operating expenses, before financing and depreciation; the standard measure of a property's earning power.
- **Assessed value / mill rate** — The value a local assessor assigns to a property, and the tax rate applied to it, quoted as dollars per $1,000 of value.
- **Adjusted basis** — Purchase price plus capital improvements minus depreciation taken; the number your sale proceeds are measured against to compute gain.
- **Depreciation recapture (unrecaptured §1250 gain)** — The portion of gain attributable to depreciation you previously deducted, taxed at up to 25% at sale.
- **Section 1031 exchange** — A swap of one investment property for another that defers capital gains tax, subject to 45-day identification and 180-day closing deadlines.

*This is an educational overview of how U.S. real estate taxation is structured, not tax advice. Rates, thresholds, and caps change with legislation and vary by state — confirm current figures with a CPA before acting.*

---

*Answers: 1 — c. NOI deliberately excludes debt service so the property can be compared independently of how it was financed. 2 — False. The 27.5-year schedule applies to the building only; land is never depreciated, which is why the purchase price must be allocated between the two. 3 — b. $300,000 + $20,000 − $50,000 = $270,000; every dollar of depreciation you take lowers your basis and therefore raises your eventual taxable gain.*
